q: What is the nominal mix (cement : sand : gravel) of Class C concrete?
ref: Nominal concrete classes (DPWH; Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate)
n: Class C is the leanest nominal mix, 1 : 3 : 6. It is used only for non-structural work.

q: How is the compressive strength of concrete normally tested?
o: By crushing standard cylinders in a testing machine
By rebounding a hammer on the fresh concrete
By weighing a cubic meter of the mix
ref: ASTM C143 (slump), C31 and C39 (cylinders); DPWH nominal concrete classes
n: Cylinders are cast from the delivered concrete, cured, and crushed at set ages (ASTM C39). The failure load divided by the cylinder area gives f'c. The slump test checks only workability.

q: How is modern structural concrete usually specified, instead of by a fixed nominal mix such as Class A?
o: By the color and source of the aggregate
By the number of cement bags per truck only
By its required strength f'c, with a designed mix
By the slump alone, with no strength stated
ref: ASTM C143 (slump), C31 and C39 (cylinders); DPWH nominal concrete classes
n: Nominal mixes like 1 : 2 : 4 are simple prescriptions. Engineered work specifies f'c (for example 28 MPa) and durability limits, and the supplier designs and tests a mix to meet them.

q: At what age is the specified compressive strength f'c of concrete normally measured?
ref: ASTM C143 (slump), C31 and C39 (cylinders); DPWH nominal concrete classes
n: 28 days is the standard age: most strength has developed by then. Some mixes with slow-gaining cements may be specified at 56 or 90 days.

q: How is the slump cone filled during a slump test?
o: In three layers of about equal volume, each rodded 25 times
In two layers, each vibrated with a poker
In five layers, each tamped once
ref: ASTM C143
n: Each of the three layers is rodded 25 times with a 16 mm bullet-nosed rod, the rod just reaching into the layer below. The top is struck off level before the cone is lifted.

q: What is the standard size of a concrete test cylinder?
o: 150 mm diameter × 300 mm high (6 in × 12 in)
150 mm cube, as in British practice
ref: ASTM C31 / C39
n: The standard cylinder is 150 × 300 mm. Smaller 100 × 200 mm cylinders are also allowed. Cubes are used in British and European practice, not in ASTM testing.

q: In the slump test, how quickly is the cone lifted?
o: As fast as possible, in under 1 second
Straight up in about 5 seconds (5 ± 2 s)
With a twisting motion over 30 seconds
ref: ASTM C143
n: The cone is raised steadily straight up in 5 ± 2 seconds, with no twisting. The whole test, from filling to lifting, should take no more than 2½ minutes.

q: When are freshly made concrete cylinders normally taken out of their molds?
ref: ASTM C31
n: ASTM C31 calls for demolding after 24 ± 8 hours, then curing (usually in lime-saturated water) until testing.

q: In a slump test, how is the slump measured?
o: As the drop from the top of the cone to the top of the settled concrete
As the spread of the concrete across the base plate
As the height of the settled concrete
As the weight of the concrete
ref: ASTM C143
n: The cone is set beside the slumped concrete and the drop is measured at the displaced original center of the top surface, to the nearest 5 mm.

q: A concrete test cylinder is 150 mm in diameter and follows the standard 2:1 height-to-diameter ratio. What is its height?
ref: ASTM C143 (slump), C31 and C39 (cylinders); DPWH nominal concrete classes
n: Standard cylinders are twice as tall as they are wide: 2 × 150 = 300 mm.

q: In the common Philippine slump table, what maximum slump is recommended for beams and reinforced walls?
ref: Philippine construction slump table (older public-works specification)
n: Beams and reinforced walls allow a slightly wetter mix, 7.5 cm, so concrete can flow around the bars.

q: Which use is Class AA concrete normally specified for?
o: Slabs on fill and non-bearing walls
Concrete placed under water and retaining walls
ref: Nominal concrete classes (DPWH; Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate)
n: Class AA is the richest nominal mix (1 : 1½ : 3). It is kept for demanding work such as underwater concrete, retaining walls and thin, heavily reinforced members.

q: In the common Philippine slump table, what maximum slump is recommended for tops of walls, piers, parapets and curbs?
ref: Philippine construction slump table (older public-works specification)
n: Tops of walls, piers, parapets and curbs are kept stiff (5.0 cm) so the concrete holds its shape at exposed edges.

q: Which use is Class A concrete normally specified for?
o: Concrete placed under water and retaining walls
Footings, columns, beams and reinforced concrete slabs
Concrete plant boxes and fill concrete
Slabs on fill and non-bearing walls
ref: Nominal concrete classes (DPWH; Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate)
n: Class A (1 : 2 : 4) is the everyday structural mix for footings, columns, beams and suspended slabs.

q: In the common Philippine slump table, what maximum slump is recommended for canal linings?
ref: Philippine construction slump table (older public-works specification)
n: Canal linings take 7.5 cm, wet enough to place on slopes and finish, but stiff enough not to slide down.

q: Which use is Class B concrete normally specified for?
o: Slabs on fill and non-bearing walls
ref: Nominal concrete classes (DPWH; Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate)
n: Class B (1 : 2½ : 5) is a leaner mix for lightly loaded work like slabs on fill and non-bearing walls.

q: Why do specifications set a maximum slump for each kind of work?
o: Too much water raises slump but lowers strength and durability
A higher slump always makes concrete stronger
Slump has no effect on the finished concrete
To make the concrete set faster
ref: ASTM C143 (slump), C31 and C39 (cylinders); DPWH nominal concrete classes
n: Each litre of extra water raises the water-cement ratio and so lowers strength, adds shrinkage and makes the concrete more porous. The slump limit keeps the mix only as wet as placement requires.

q: Which use is Class C concrete normally specified for?
o: Concrete plant boxes and similar non-structural work
ref: Nominal concrete classes (DPWH; Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate)
n: Class C (1 : 3 : 6) is too weak for structural use and is kept for items like plant boxes and fill concrete.

q: What are 7-day cylinder tests mainly used for?
o: As the official test used to accept or reject the concrete
To measure the slump of the concrete when delivered
As an early indication of whether the concrete will reach its 28-day strength
To find the air content of the fresh concrete
ref: ASTM C143 (slump), C31 and C39 (cylinders); DPWH nominal concrete classes
n: Ordinary portland cement concrete usually reaches about 65 to 70% of its 28-day strength at 7 days. A low 7-day result is an early warning, but acceptance is still based on the 28-day tests.

q: What is the purpose of the slump test?
o: To find the compressive strength of the hardened concrete
To measure the air content of the fresh concrete
To find how long the concrete takes to set
To check the consistency of fresh concrete and whether it meets the specified slump
ref: ASTM C143 (slump), C31 and C39 (cylinders); DPWH nominal concrete classes
n: It is a quick field check that each batch has the right consistency. A change in slump from batch to batch usually means the water content has changed.

q: Why must a test cylinder have a height about twice its diameter?
o: Short specimens test stronger because of end friction
To save concrete when casting the specimens
So that the cylinder fits inside the slump cone
Because taller specimens cure faster than short ones
ref: ASTM C143 (slump), C31 and C39 (cylinders); DPWH nominal concrete classes
n: Friction at the platens confines the ends of a specimen. In a 2:1 cylinder the middle is far enough from the ends to fail in true compression. Short specimens give higher, misleading strengths.

q: What is used to rod the concrete in the slump test?
o: A 16 mm diameter steel rod with a rounded (hemispherical) tip
A poker vibrator dipped into each layer
A steel trowel pressed onto the surface
ref: ASTM C143
n: The tamping rod is a straight 16 mm (5/8 in) steel rod about 600 mm long with a rounded end, so it compacts without cutting the layer.

q: Which ASTM standard covers the compressive strength test of concrete cylinders?
ref: ASTM C143 (slump), C31 and C39 (cylinders); DPWH nominal concrete classes
n: ASTM C39 is the cylinder compression test. C143 is the slump test, C33 covers aggregates, and D1557 is the modified Proctor compaction test for soils.

q: What is the shape of the slump cone?
o: A closed cylinder with a lid
A cube that is open at the top
A cone with a pointed top
A frustum of a cone, open at both ends
ref: ASTM C143 (slump), C31 and C39 (cylinders); DPWH nominal concrete classes
n: The mold is a hollow frustum, 300 mm high, 200 mm across the base and 100 mm across the top, open at both ends so it can be lifted off the concrete.

q: A concrete is specified at 3,000 psi. About what is that in MPa?
ref: ASTM C143 (slump), C31 and C39 (cylinders); DPWH nominal concrete classes
n: 1 MPa ≈ 145 psi, so 3,000 / 145 ≈ 20.7 MPa, usually rounded to 21 MPa. 2,500 psi is about 17 MPa and 4,000 psi about 28 MPa.

q: After the cone is lifted, the concrete drops from 300 mm to 225 mm high. What is the slump?
ref: ASTM C143 (slump), C31 and C39 (cylinders); DPWH nominal concrete classes
n: Slump is the drop, not the remaining height: 300 − 225 = 75 mm.
formula: Slump = cone height − height of slumped concrete

q: What is the nominal mix (cement : sand : gravel) of Class AA concrete?
ref: Nominal concrete classes (DPWH; Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate)
n: Class AA is the richest nominal mix, 1 : 1½ : 3, for underwater work and retaining walls.

q: In the common Philippine slump table, what maximum slump is recommended for slabs and tunnel inverts?
ref: Philippine construction slump table (older public-works specification)
n: Slabs and tunnel inverts are placed flat and need little flow, so 5.0 cm is enough and limits bleeding and shrinkage.

q: What is the nominal mix (cement : sand : gravel) of Class A concrete?
ref: Nominal concrete classes (DPWH; Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate)
n: Class A, 1 : 2 : 4, is the standard mix for footings, columns, beams and suspended slabs.

q: In the common Philippine slump table, what maximum slump is recommended for tunnel side walls and arches?
ref: Philippine construction slump table (older public-works specification)
n: Tunnel side walls and arches are high, enclosed pours that are hard to vibrate, so a wetter 10.0 cm mix is allowed to fill the forms.

q: What is the nominal mix (cement : sand : gravel) of Class B concrete?
ref: Nominal concrete classes (DPWH; Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate)
n: Class B, 1 : 2½ : 5, is for slabs on fill and non-bearing walls.

q: In the common Philippine slump table, what maximum slump is recommended for heavy mass construction?
ref: Philippine construction slump table (older public-works specification)
n: Mass concrete is kept stiff (5.0 cm) because extra water adds heat of hydration and shrinkage in thick pours.
